title: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free? (part 1 of 4)
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md (K2, K3: count and its spoilers)
sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md (C14: real and fictitious threats; paraphrased as the idea that a piece left en prise can be safe for a while)
docs/lesson-depth-standard.md class A; positions authored and engine-checked in content/items/lesson-bg-l-saf-loose-1.json; opening moves replayed with python-chess

steps.text: Your rook just took a knight, and Black could not take back. In this course that knight was **loose**: an enemy piece attacked it, and none of its own side's pieces defended it. A loose piece can be taken for free. Missing a free piece, yours or theirs, is one of the most common ways a game swings. [H] I suspect it is the most common cause below club level, but I have not measured it.

steps.caption: The rook looks up the d-file at a knight that has no friend beside it or behind it.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. No black piece guards d5, so nothing can take the rook back.
Black has no recapture. A whole knight is gone for nothing.

claims.statement: Only the knight on d5 is loose.
No black piece defends the knight.
Taking the knight wins it for nothing.

steps.caption: Same rook, same knight, but now a pawn on e6 defends it. Attacked is not the same as loose.

line.say: The pawn takes back. White gave a rook for a knight, a bad trade.

claims.statement: The pawn on e6 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses the rook for a knight.

steps.text: In this course a piece is **loose** when two things are true: an enemy piece **attacks** it, and no friendly piece **defends** it. Attacked but defended is not loose: they take back. Many coaches call any undefended piece loose and use *hanging* for the attacked kind [R: recalled usage, no source read]. We keep the two states apart. Undefended but not attacked is not free yet, and the next board shows why it still matters.

steps.caption: [I] Nothing is loose yet, but the rook on b4 and the bishop on f6 are both undefended. One knight move attacks both: undefended pieces are the targets of double attacks.

line.say: The knight jumps to d5 and attacks the rook and the bishop at once. Neither has a guard.
The knight takes the bishop with check.

claims.statement: Before the move no black piece is loose.
After the knight move both are loose.
The fork is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: Three black pieces to sort. Bishop: attacked, no guard, so loose. Knight: attacked but guarded. Rook: no guard, but not attacked.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop. Nothing guards g4, so nothing takes the pawn back.

claims.statement: Only the bishop on g4 is loose.
The pawn on e6 defends the knight.
Nothing attacks the rook on a8.
Taking the bishop is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: Any piece can be the attacker, even a pawn. Here the pawn attacks a knight that no black piece guards.

line.say: A pawn is worth little, yet it takes the knight. Nothing recaptures.
White has won a whole knight for nothing.

claims.statement: The knight on d6 is loose.
Taking the knight is the engine's best move.

steps.text: **Remember.** A piece is loose when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side defends it, so it can be taken for free. Attacked but defended is not loose, and undefended but not attacked is not free yet. After each move, ask: what is attacked, and who defends it? Even a pawn can be the attacker.
